A harrow is a farm tool dragged over plowed ground to break up lumps; a gizzard is a muscular stomach that grinds food with sand or grit. Amendments are things added to improve soil, such as lime; fertilizers feed plants; drainage carries away extra water. An agriculturist is a farmer.

excerpt.locator: “The Earthworm,” Teacher’s Story, the first two paragraphs; opens “The earthworm is, among lower animals, essentially the farmer. Long before man conceived…”; closes “…plants by cultivating, that is keeping fine and granular, the soil about the roots.”.

questions.prompt: What does Comstock call the earthworm in the first sentence? Why does she say it was there first?
facilitatorNotes: “Essentially the farmer.” It was plowing, harrowing and fertilizing the land “long before man conceived the idea of tilling the soil.”
evidence: The earthworm is, among lower animals, essentially the farmer.
Long before man conceived the idea of tilling the soil,

questions.prompt: How does the earthworm “plow” and “harrow”?
facilitatorNotes: It plows by bringing subsoil up from deep down; it harrows by grinding soil in its sand-filled gizzard, making it finer than a rake can.
evidence: bringing to the surface the subsoil, which is exactly what we do when we plow deeply.
the earthworm grinds it in a gizzard stocked with grains of sand or fine gravel,

questions.prompt: Name two more farm jobs the earthworm does, and how.
facilitatorNotes: Fertilizing (dragging leaves, flowers and bones into its burrows, where they decay); drainage (boring holes that carry off water); planting (covering seeds with soil); cultivating (keeping soil fine round roots).
evidence: They plant seeds by covering those that lie on the ground with soil from below the surface
but they bore holes to some depth which carry off the surplus water.

questions.prompt: Comstock uses one comparison, the worm as farmer, all the way through. Why is that a good way to teach about earthworms? Does the comparison go too far anywhere?
facilitatorNotes: Readers already know what a farmer does, so each job makes the worm’s work clear and important. But worms do not plan: “have never studied any system of drainage” admits it. Some may think “adept in the use of fertilizers” goes too far.
evidence: These minute agriculturists have never studied any system of drainage,
The earthworm is apparently an adept in the use of fertilizers;

readings.title: The Crayfish — a nest dug in the aquarium (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow a crayfish’s movements exactly, and notice when the writer gives it human feelings.
readings.focus: Watching closely makes a crayfish’s digging look like human work, and its quarrels like human tempers.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Its nippers are claws; its jaw-feet are small limbs near the mouth; debris is loose rubble; a quadruped walks on four feet; profanity is swearing.

excerpt.locator: “The Crayfish,” Teacher’s Story, last two paragraphs; opens “I have been greatly entertained by watching a female crayfish make her nest in my…”; closes “…how constantly the larger pair of jaw-feet are used to help pick up and carry the loads.”.

questions.prompt: How does the crayfish start digging her nest?
facilitatorNotes: At one side of the tank she pushes her feelers and nippers down between the glass and the stones, grabs a pebble in each claw and pulls it up.
evidence: she seizes a pebble in each claw and pulls it up

questions.prompt: Comstock compares the crayfish to a lady and to a schoolboy. What is each comparison describing?
facilitatorNotes: Tucking her tail under her body is like a lady tucking up her skirts for work; holding the load down with her jaw-feet is like a schoolboy steadying a pile of books with his chin.
evidence: as a lady tucks up her skirts
just as I have seen a schoolboy use his chin,

questions.prompt: What does the crayfish’s tail “say” when she drops her load? How can a tail say anything?
facilitatorNotes: “There!” The tail snaps straight as she lets go. Comstock is reading the gesture as a word, the way people read each other’s body language.
evidence: her tail straightens out with a gesture which says plainly, “There!”

questions.prompt: What does one crayfish do with the earthworm she is given? Which words describe what happened, and which describe what Comstock thinks the crayfish felt?
facilitatorNotes: She carries the worm and a pebble to the other nest and throws both on her neighbor, who rears up waving his claws. “Seized,” “glided” and “threw down” describe actions; “spitefully” and “crayfish profanity” are Comstock’s guesses at feelings. Readers can decide whether the guesses seem fair.
evidence: spitefully threw down both worm and pebble on top of her fellow prisoner,
the most eloquent of crayfish profanity.

readings.title: Daddy-Longlegs — legs that feel the world (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Imagine being a creature whose legs are its fingers and feelers.
readings.focus: The daddy-longlegs explores with its second pair of legs and tests food with its palpi.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. A daddy-longlegs (also called a harvestman) has eight very long, thin legs; it is related to spiders but is not one. The water’s surface film is the thin “skin” that lets light things rest on water. Palpi (one is a palpus) are small leg-like feelers beside the mouth.

excerpt.locator: “Daddy-Longlegs, or Grandfather Greybeard,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraphs on the legs and walking; opens “I have seen a “daddy” walk into a drop of water and his foot was never wetted, so light…”; closes “…wishes to test a substance. The end segment of the palpus is tipped with a single claw.”.

questions.prompt: What did Comstock see when a daddy-longlegs walked into a drop of water?
facilitatorNotes: Its foot never got wet, because it touched the water’s surface so lightly.
evidence: I have seen a “daddy” walk into a drop of water and his foot was never wetted,

questions.prompt: Which legs are longest, and what are they used for?
facilitatorNotes: The second pair. They explore the surroundings; when he runs, he spreads them wide and keeps them moving, feeling things by touch.
evidence: The legs of the second pair are ordinarily used in exploring the surroundings.
these two legs are spread wide apart and keep in rapid motion;

questions.prompt: How long would your legs be if they were as long, for your size, as a daddy-longlegs’ legs? Why does Comstock give this comparison?
facilitatorNotes: About forty feet. It explains why the creature moves so fast, and makes its strange shape easy to imagine.
evidence: If our legs were as long in comparison as his, they would be about forty feet in length.

questions.prompt: When the long legs sense food, the daddy-longlegs changes how it moves. Describe it. Why does it move this way?
facilitatorNotes: It teeters, tipping its body down at every step, so its palpi can explore the ground below; it can stretch them out to test a substance. Readers may compare it with how they would check a strange food.
evidence: he commences a peculiar teetering motion of the body,
they can be extended out quite a distance if “daddy” wishes to test a substance.

readings.title: The Hepatica — a flower that faces the sun (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Decide whether names matter, and find what makes a small flower seem brave.
readings.focus: One of the first wildflowers of spring talks back to the scientists and stands up to the snow.

Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The hepatica is one of the first wildflowers of spring in the woods of eastern North America, with pale blue, pink or white flowers above leathery three-lobed leaves. The first paragraph is a passage Comstock quotes from a children’s book of wild flowers. Sepals are the small leaf-like parts that wrap a flower bud; petals are usually the colorful parts; bracts are small leaves just below a flower. Sodden means soaked; glacial means icy; an optical delusion is a trick of the eyes. The acanthus is a plant whose leaves were carved on ancient Greek columns; tapestries are woven wall-hangings.

excerpt.locator: “The Hepatica,” Teacher’s Story, the first two paragraphs; opens ““The wise men say the hepatica flower has no petals but has pink, white or purple sepals…”; closes “…to the snow-drifts, looking out on a gray-brown world, nodding to it and calling it good.”.

questions.prompt: What do “the wise men” say about the hepatica’s flower? What does the hepatica answer?
facilitatorNotes: That it has no petals, only colored sepals, and that the three leaflets below are bracts. The hepatica answers that the bees do not care what the parts are called, and asks why it should not wear its pretty “petticoat” as a dress.
evidence: the hepatica flower has no petals but has pink, white or purple sepals instead:
Since my petticoat is pretty enough for a dress why should not I wear it thus?

questions.prompt: Does it matter what we call the parts of a flower? Who is right, the wise men or the hepatica?
facilitatorNotes: Both have a point: exact names help scientists compare plants, but the parts do the same job, showing bees where the pollen is. Let readers argue.
evidence: The bees do not care whether they are sepals or petals since they are pretty in color, and show where the pollen is to be found.

questions.prompt: Why does Comstock go looking for hepaticas? What are the woods like?
facilitatorNotes: A longing for spring wakes with the first warm sunshine. The woods are soaked, with streams and puddles fed by snowdrifts still heaped on the north side of things.
evidence: because there is a longing for spring in our hearts that awakens with the first warm sunshine.
having their sources in the snow-drifts still heaped on the north side of things,

questions.prompt: Why does the flower at first seem like “an optical delusion”?
facilitatorNotes: A speck of pale blue or pink-purple among all the browns is so unexpected that she has to look again to be sure.
evidence: a bit of pale-blue or pink-purple that at first seems like an optical delusion;

questions.prompt: What makes these flowers “brave”? What do they seem to say about the gray-brown world?
facilitatorNotes: They face the sun with their backs to the snowdrifts and nod to the gray-brown world, “calling it good,” as if they believe in spring before anyone else does.
evidence: these brave little flowers stand with their faces to the sun and their backs to the snow-drifts,
nodding to it and calling it good.

readings.title: The Evening Primrose — a flower that opens at dusk (excerpt)

readings.focus: The sudden opening of a flower at evening, watched closely and timed.

facilitatorNotes: On a warm evening, usually about sunset (anywhere from four o’clock to nine or ten). For two or three days the long tube turns yellow and a row of petals pushes up between the sepals.
evidence: Then some warm evening, usually about sunset,
the long tube which looks like the flower stem has been turning yellow;

questions.prompt: How does the umbrella comparison help explain why one petal seems to do all the work?
facilitatorNotes: The petals are wrapped round each other like a folded umbrella, so one petal’s edge comes free first and seems to lead, though all of them are pushing.
evidence: they are wrapped around each other in the bud as an umbrella is folded,

evidence: all the others are pushing for freedom;
which seem to try to repress them.

evidence: the way each extreme tip is bent into a hook
when during its graceful swaying the hook catches to some object, it makes fast with amazing rapidity;

questions.prompt: Which way does bindweed twine? What does it do when it has nothing to climb, or only something wobbly?

evidence: following the direction of the hands of the clock
they twist until so hard-twisted that they form a support in themselves.

evidence: we first admire its beautiful shape;
suggests embossed embroidery.

questions.prompt: What three things are inside the pod?

the exquisite milkweed silk

no human reel could give us a skein of such luster.

my tongue smarted and burned for some time after,

No wonder my cheeks were red one day and purple the next,

reached below most other plants for moisture and food.

can hear them crackle as they spring back.

Away from each other this double procession moves,

evidence: how it knows just where to begin is more than we can tell.
we may find all stages of this blossoming in the flower-heads of one plant.

readings.title: The Pumpkin — two kinds of flowers and their treasure (excerpt)

readings.focus: A pumpkin grows only when bees carry pollen from one kind of blossom to the other.

questions.prompt: How can you tell which pumpkin flower will become a pumpkin?
facilitatorNotes: It has a little green globe, the ovary, below it.
evidence: selecting a flower that has below it a little green globe—the ovary—which will later develop into a pumpkin.

questions.prompt: What do the stigmas look like, and what must a bee do to reach the nectar in that flower?
facilitatorNotes: Like tiny boxing-gloves on posts. The bee must “stand on her head” and brush her pollen-dusty side against them.
evidence: three stigmas, that look like liliputian boxing-gloves;
the lady bee must stand on her head

questions.prompt: Some people said bees visit the other kind of flower only for pollen. What did Comstock find?

we shall find below the latter, a treasure cave;

as this is the only way that the fruit may be developed.

readings.title: The Chestnut — stars of yellow chenille (excerpt)

excerpt.locator: “The Chestnut,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraph on the blossoms; opens “The chestnut is always a beautiful tree, whether green in summer or glowing golden yellow…”; closes “…of the catkins in a blossom-star, we get a glimmering of the amount of pollen produced.”.

questions.prompt: When is the chestnut most beautiful, and what does it look like then?
facilitatorNotes: In late June and July, when it is covered with pale yellow “stars.”
evidence: it is most beautiful during late June and July, when covered with constellations of pale yellow stars.

questions.prompt: What is each “star” made of? Why does it look like chenille?
facilitatorNotes: Each is a rosette of catkins six or eight inches long; tufts of tiny stamens stand out all along each catkin like the fuzz on chenille yarn.
evidence: each ray consists of a catkin often six or eight inches in length, looking like a thread of yellowish chenille fringe,
No wonder it looks like chenille!

questions.prompt: Comstock estimated the stamens in one catkin. If a star has thirty catkins, about how many stamens does it have? Why does she not finish the sum?

evidence: In one catkin I estimated that there were approximately 2,500 stamens developed,
we get a glimmering of the amount of pollen produced.

questions.prompt: Why might a tree make so much pollen? What does it tell you about how hard it is for pollen to reach a flower?

evidence: each anther packed with pollen.

questions.prompt: When is the brook doing the least work, and when is it working hardest?
facilitatorNotes: Least when its water is perfectly clear; hardest when it is “roily,” usually after rain.
evidence: when its waters are perfectly clear—the stream is doing the least work.
when the waters are roily the brook is working very hard.

questions.prompt: Poets talk about the brook “playing.” What does Comstock say it is really doing?
facilitatorNotes: Digging and carrying: each drop snatches up a little earth and uses it to knock loose more. The muddy water shows the load.
evidence: it is a very busy worker, its chief labor being that of a digger and carrier.
snatches up a tiny load of earth and carries it along.

questions.prompt: What happens when the brook reaches level ground? In what order does it drop its load?
facilitatorNotes: The drops “act tired” and let their loads fall: gravel and rocks first, fine soil last and farthest.
evidence: the drops act tired and seem to have no ambition to pick up more soil,
the gravel is always dropped first, and that the fine mud is carried farthest

questions.prompt: Comstock calls the brook “a gang of workmen each of which is using its own load as a tool.” How does this picture help explain why a flood digs so much? Can you think of another picture for it?

evidence: On and on the brook flows, a gang of workmen each of which is using its own load as a tool,
uses its own little load of earth or gravel as a crowbar or pickaxe

A telescope makes faraway things look nearer; a spectroscope splits starlight into colors and shows what a star is made of. An orbit is the path one body travels around another. The Pole-star is the North Star; the Pleiades are a small cluster of stars.

excerpt.locator: “The Story of the Stars,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraphs on what the stars are and how far away they are; opens “Thus, we have learned many things about the stars; we know that every shining star is a…”; closes “…was discovered. Most of the stars are so far away that we cannot measure the distance.”.

questions.prompt: What does Comstock say every shining star really is? What did she think some stars might have?
facilitatorNotes: A great blazing sun. She thought many might have worlds like the earth spinning round them, too far away to see. Since the 1990s astronomers have found thousands of such planets.
evidence: we know that every shining star is a great blazing sun,
there is no reason to doubt that many of these suns have worlds, like the earth, spinning around them

questions.prompt: What is a double star? How long do different pairs take to circle each other?
facilitatorNotes: Two suns that swing round a common center but look like one star. Some take five years, others sixteen or forty-six, one “lazy pair” about sixteen hundred, and some only a few hours.
evidence: made up of two vast suns swinging around a common center;
there is at least one lazy pair which seems to require fully sixteen hundred years

questions.prompt: What is a light-year, and why do astronomers use it?
facilitatorNotes: The distance light travels in a year, about six trillion miles. Distances in miles are too large to grasp.
evidence: this distance is called a light-year.
when this distance is expressed in miles it is too much for us to grasp.

questions.prompt: Comstock says the light from the Pole-star left it “almost half a century ago.” Astronomers now measure it as over four hundred years. What does that tell you about reading an old science book? Why is it still worth reading?
facilitatorNotes: Measurements improve, so numbers in old books may be out of date; check them against newer sources. But her main idea is still right: starlight is old light, and looking at a star is looking into the past. Readers may find that idea the most amazing part.
evidence: the light which reaches our eyes left that star almost half a century ago,
the light we get from the Pleiades may have started on its journey before America was discovered.

readings.title: The Pole-star and the Dippers — finding the North Star (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow directions that you can test on the next clear night.
readings.focus: The Big Dipper’s pointers lead to the North Star, which stays in our sky all night.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The Big Dipper is a group of seven bright stars shaped like a long-handled cup. The earth’s axis is the imaginary line it spins around, through the North and South Poles. The Northern Hemisphere is the half of the earth north of the equator. A mariner’s compass is a sailor’s compass; a coincidence is two things that happen together by chance.

excerpt.locator: “The Pole-star and the Dippers,” Teacher’s Story, the first paragraph; opens “The way to begin star study is to learn to know the Big Dipper, and through its pointers…”; closes “…to be nearly in the direction toward which the northern end of the compass needle points.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Comstock say star study should begin with the Big Dipper and the Pole-star?
facilitatorNotes: They give a fixed starting point for finding any other star.
evidence: so as to have some fixed point to start from.

questions.prompt: How do you find the Pole-star from the Big Dipper? Try drawing it.
facilitatorNotes: Draw a line through the two outer stars of the bowl and continue it: it reaches the Pole-star. These two are called the pointers.
evidence: A line drawn through the outer two stars of the bowl, if extended, will touch the North Star, or Pole-star.

questions.prompt: Why does the Pole-star never set for people in the Northern Hemisphere? Is there a South Pole-star?
facilitatorNotes: The northern end of the earth’s axis points almost straight at it, so it stays above the North Pole while the sky seems to turn. There is no convenient South Pole-star.
evidence: the northern end of the earth’s axis is directed toward it,
so there is no South Pole-star.

questions.prompt: Comstock says twice that something is only a coincidence. What are the two coincidences? Why does she bother to point them out?
facilitatorNotes: That the Pole-star lies where the earth’s axis points, and that a compass needle points nearly toward it. She wants readers not to think the star pulls on the earth or the compass; her blackboard-and-pointer comparison makes the same point. Ask why it matters not to mix up “happens together” with “causes.”
evidence: the North Star has nothing to do with the axis of our earth any more than the figure on the blackboard has to do with the pointer;
It is also a coincidence that the needle of the mariner’s compass points toward the North Star;

readings.title: The Pleiades — a misty cluster of stars (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Separate what eyes can see from what telescopes and cameras reveal, and imagine distances too big to picture.
readings.focus: A tiny smudge of stars in the winter sky that turns out to be a family of thousands.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The Pleiades are a small, close group of stars in the evening sky from late autumn through winter, near the bright reddish star Aldebaran; they are also called the Seven Sisters. A constellation is a pattern of stars; enthralled means held spellbound; a nebula is a huge cloud of gas and dust in space; infinity means endlessness. Astronomers have learned more since Comstock wrote: today they count about a thousand stars in the cluster, about 440 light-years away, and think the mist around it is a separate dust cloud the stars are passing through, not the cloud they were born from.

excerpt.locator: “Aldebaran and the Pleiades,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraph on the Pleiades; opens “Although we are attracted by many bright stars in the winter sky, yet there is a little…”; closes “…Pleiades, and much poetic imagining has been developed to account for the “lost Pleiad.””.

questions.prompt: How many stars in the Pleiades can most people see? How many did sky photography reveal?
facilitatorNotes: Most eyes count six; nine are bright enough to have names; photographs showed more than three thousand (today astronomers count about a thousand true members). On a clear winter night readers can count for themselves.
evidence: most eyes can count only six stars in the constellation.
sky photography has revealed to us that there are more than three thousand stars in this little group.

questions.prompt: What reasons did astronomers have for thinking these stars belong together?
facilitatorNotes: The mist that seems to loop between them, and the facts that they are at the same stage of life, are made of the same materials and move together in the same direction. Astronomers still think they are a family that formed together.
evidence: the stars are all in the same stage of development and have the same chemical composition, and they are all moving together in the same direction.

questions.prompt: The stars look close together. How far apart are they really? How long does their light take to reach us?
facilitatorNotes: So far apart that our sun and all its planets could roll between them unnoticed; light takes years to cross from one to another and several hundred years to reach us. The light we see tonight left them hundreds of years ago.
evidence: our own sun and all its planets could roll in between them and never be noticed.
it takes light several hundred years to reach us from them.

questions.prompt: What is the “lost Pleiad”? Why might people have made up stories about it?
facilitatorNotes: An old story says people once saw seven stars, not six, so poets invented reasons for one disappearing. The name Seven Sisters needs seven; some sharp-eyed people really can see seven or more.
evidence: once the unaided eye could see seven instead of six stars in the Pleiades,

questions.prompt: Why do the Pleiades give Comstock “a feeling of the infinity of the universe”?
facilitatorNotes: A smudge that looks tiny holds thousands of suns spread over unimaginable distances; it makes the universe feel endless. Ask readers what makes them feel small, or big, when they look at the sky.
evidence: Perhaps no stars in the heavens give us such a feeling of the infinity of the universe as do the Pleiades;

readings.title: The Moon — always half lit (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Explain the moon’s changing shapes with one simple fact, and imagine the earth seen from the moon.
readings.focus: Why the moon seems to change shape though it is always there, and lit, just the same.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story” telling what she herself had watched. Her observations are more than a hundred years old: read them as one careful watcher’s record, not a modern field guide. The phases of the moon are its changing shapes over about a month: new, crescent, quarter, full and back again. Reflected light is light that bounces off something. Earthshine is sunlight bounced off the earth onto the moon. An eclipse of the moon happens when the earth’s shadow falls on it. “The old moon in the new moon’s arms” is an old saying for a thin bright crescent with the rest of the moon faintly visible. A lamp and a ball in a dark room make a good model of the phases.

excerpt.locator: “The Moon,” Teacher’s Story, the paragraph on the moon’s phases and earthshine; opens “The moon is a member of our sun’s family, his granddaughter we might call her if the…”; closes “…moon when the earth passes between the sun and the moon, hiding the latter in its shadow.”.

questions.prompt: Why is one half of the moon always dark?
facilitatorNotes: The moon has no light of its own; it shines only by reflecting sunlight, so the half facing away from the sun is always in shadow.
evidence: since the moon has no fires or light of its own, it shines by light reflected from the sun and, therefore, one-half of it is always in shadow.

questions.prompt: Why do we call it a “quarter” moon when it looks like half a circle?
facilitatorNotes: We see half of the lighted half, and half of a half is one quarter of the whole moon.
evidence: because all we can see is one-half of one-half which is one-quarter;

questions.prompt: When we say there is “no moon,” where is it? Is its far side ever in the dark for good?
facilitatorNotes: It is still there with its lit side turned away from us. The sun shines on every side of it in turn, even the side we never see.
evidence: we say there is no moon, although it is always there just the same.
the sun shines on all sides of it.

questions.prompt: What would the earth look like from the moon? How does that explain “the old moon in the new moon’s arms”?
facilitatorNotes: A splendid “moon” almost four times as wide as ours. Sunlight bouncing off the earth faintly lights the dark part of the moon beside the bright crescent.
evidence: Think what a splendid moon our earth must seem to the lady in the moon!
is visible because of the earthshine reflected from it.

questions.prompt: How is “the old moon in the new moon’s arms” different from an eclipse?
facilitatorNotes: It happens at a thin crescent, when the moon is near the sun in our sky. An eclipse of the moon can happen only at full moon, when the earth passes between the sun and the moon and its shadow covers the moon.
evidence: an eclipse must always occur at the full of the moon when the earth passes between the sun and the moon,

readings.title: The Maize, or Indian Corn — the first Americans’ golden treasure (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Notice who speaks first, and how Comstock links their corn to Columbus and to the first colonists.
readings.focus: An Iroquois prayer of thanks opens the story of maize, the corn that peoples of the Americas grew long before Columbus and that kept the first colonists alive.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story.” Maize is the first Americans’ name for corn. The Iroquois, who call themselves the Haudenosaunee, are a league of nations whose lands lie in what is now New York State; Ha-wen-ni-yu is their name for the Great Spirit, and He-no is the Thunderer, who brings rain. In 1492 Christopher Columbus sailed west looking for the Indies, the lands of Asia rich in cloth and spices; his ships’ prows are their fronts. Columbus Day remembers his landing in the Americas, and many places now keep the day as Indigenous Peoples’ Day too, honoring peoples such as the Iroquois who were here first. Colonists are settlers from Europe; to girdle a tree is to cut a ring through its bark so that its top dies; tillage is plowing and digging.
readings.contentNote: Comstock writes, as people did in her time, that America was “first discovered” when Europeans arrived, though its peoples had lived and farmed here for thousands of years, and she calls them Indians.

excerpt.locator: “The Maize, or Indian Corn,” the opening of the Teacher’s Story, from the Iroquois prayer to the colonists’ corn; opens ““Hail! Ha-wen-ni-yu! Listen with open ears to the words of thy people. Continue to…”; closes “…they might have starved before they gained a foothold on our forest-covered shores.”.

questions.prompt: Who is praying in the first paragraph? List the things they give thanks for.
facilitatorNotes: The Iroquois, when their corn was ripe. They thank the earth, the winds that drove away sickness, He-no for rain, the moon and stars, the sun, and the Great Spirit for making the corn grow.
evidence: We thank our mother earth which sustains us.
We thank thee that thou hast made our corn to grow.

questions.prompt: Columbus was looking for the Indies and their “fabrics and spices.” What does Comstock say was worth more than anything he could have found there?
facilitatorNotes: The ripe corn, which she calls a “golden treasure.” It was growing on the hills of New York long before he sailed, cared for by the Iroquois.
evidence: even before Columbus had turned his ambitious prows westward in quest of the Indies
nothing so valuable to the world as has proved this golden treasure of ripened corn

questions.prompt: Why could the first colonists grow corn when wheat and rye were hard to grow? Who had been growing it, and for how long?
facilitatorNotes: Corn needed no plowing or clearing: kill the treetops by girdling, scratch the earth, plant the seed, and the plants took care of themselves. Wheat and rye need well-plowed fields. The American Indians had grown maize for so long that it was fully a farm plant before any Europeans came.
evidence: No plowing, nor even clearing, was necessary for the successful raising of this grain.
so long had maize been cultivated by the American Indians that it was thoroughly domesticated

questions.prompt: Comstock says the colonists might have starved without Indian corn. What does that tell you about the meeting of the people who lived here and the people who came across the sea? Why might some people keep this day as Indigenous Peoples’ Day?
facilitatorNotes: The newcomers lived on a crop, and on knowledge, that the peoples already here had developed over many lifetimes. Remembering only the voyage leaves out the people who fed the newcomers. Some families keep both names for the day; children can say what each name asks us to remember.
evidence: if our forefathers could have remained here had it not been for Indian corn
they might have starved before they gained a foothold on our forest-covered shores

readings.title: The Pumpkin — Whittier’s Thanksgiving pie (excerpt)
readings.author: John Greenleaf Whittier
readings.challenge: Find the two times of life this poem remembers, and what a pumpkin has to do with both.
readings.focus: A poet remembers families coming home for Thanksgiving and his own autumns as a boy, all called back by a taste of pumpkin pie.
readings.context: Anna Botsford Comstock (1854–1930) was a naturalist and artist who taught nature study at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Her Handbook of Nature-Study (1911) was written for teachers, and each lesson opens with a “Teacher’s Story.” She ended her lesson on the pumpkin with two stanzas from “The Pumpkin,” a poem by John Greenleaf Whittier (1807–1892), who grew up on a Massachusetts farm. Thanksgiving, a day of thanks for the harvest, was the great family holiday of New England, when grown children traveled home. A pilgrim here is a traveler; the board is the dinner table; a matron is a grown woman with a family; wood-grapes are wild grapes; a corn-heap is a pile of corn waiting to have its husks pulled off. The fairy with the pumpkin coach and a team of rats is Cinderella’s fairy godmother.

excerpt.locator: “The Pumpkin,” the two stanzas of Whittier’s poem quoted at the end of the lesson; opens “Ah! on Thanksgiving day, when from East and from West, From North and from South come the…”; closes “—J. G. Whittier.”.

questions.prompt: Who comes to the table on Thanksgiving day, and from where? Find two people who have grown older.
facilitatorNotes: Travelers and guests from every direction, East, West, North and South. The gray-haired New Englander sees his family around him; a tired man comes back to his mother; a worn woman smiles in the place where she smiled as a girl.
evidence: From North and from South come the pilgrim and guest,
When the care-wearied man seeks his mother once more,
And the worn matron smiles where the girl smiled before,

questions.prompt: “The old broken lines of affection restored.” What had been broken, and how does Thanksgiving mend it?
facilitatorNotes: The family circle, broken when children grew up and moved far away, like a chain with missing links or a table with empty chairs. On Thanksgiving everyone comes home and the circle is whole again.
evidence: The old broken lines of affection restored,

questions.prompt: In the second stanza, what did the boy and his friends do with pumpkins? Which of those things do people still do in autumn?
facilitatorNotes: They carved wild, ugly faces in pumpkins and lit them with candles, sat on pumpkins around the corn-heap while husking under the moon, and told the fairy tale of the pumpkin coach. Jack-o’-lanterns and fall stories are still part of autumn.
evidence: When wild, ugly faces we carved in its skin,
Our chair a broad pumpkin—our lantern the moon,

questions.prompt: The first stanza asks, “What calls back the past, like the rich Pumpkin pie?” Why might a taste bring back memories? Is the poem happy, sad, or both?
facilitatorNotes: Tastes and smells are tied to the times we met them, so one bite of pie can return a grown-up to the table of his childhood and to the people who were there. The poem is glad, but “moistens the lip and brightens the eye” may hint at tears as well as smiles; the gray hair and worn faces remember people and years that are gone.
evidence: What moistens the lip and brightens the eye?
Oh, fruit loved of boyhood! the old days recalling,
